fatal_errors: The hypothesis invents minor alloying additions and grain-boundary precipitates that were not part of the equimolar WTaTiVZr material.
It misses the observed two-BCC, solidification-segregated dendritic structure comprising W-Ta-rich dendrites and Zr-Ti-rich interdendritic regions.
The proposed mechanism is supported only by evidence concerning boron-modified HfMoNbTaTiZr, a compositionally and microstructurally different alloy.
The controlled comparison changes alloy composition rather than comparing the as-cast equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy with commercially used powder-sintered tungsten under matched tests.
The claimed service boundary implies operating plasma-facing-component conditions, although irradiation and in-reactor fusion service were not tested.
explanation: The response identifies the general question of plastic strain and toughness relative to pure tungsten and predicts improvement in both, but it does not reconstruct the tested material, intervention, conditions, or inferred mechanism. The target alloy contained no intentional minor-element addition or demonstrated grain-boundary precipitate population. Its behavior was instead interpreted through multicomponent solid-solution strengthening, lattice distortion, W/Ta-associated frictional resistance, and Ti/V/Zr-associated changes in dislocation behavior, cohesion, localized plasticity, and crack propagation within a segregated two-BCC dendritic microstructure. The cited paper discusses boride precipitation after adding boron to HfMoNbTaTiZr and therefore cannot establish precipitation as the governing cause in equimolar WTaTiVZr. The proposed experiment could test a separate alloy-design hypothesis, but it would not isolate the cause of the reported WTaTiVZr-versus-tungsten difference and omits the relevant compression, temperature-dependent indentation, and scratch-toughness conditions and quantitative predictions.
